summary: Brad Gerstner bought more OpenAI shares and sees both OpenAI and Anthropic as among the most important companies in the history of capitalism, with strong revenue momentum and a need to go public to access cheap capital for compute buildout.

summary: Chamath questions the durability and quality of Anthropic's revenue, arguing much of it is experimental checkbox spending rather than production-critical workflows, and criticizes leadership's inconsistent messaging as a risk to the business.
quote: I am paying these models millions of dollars a year. And what I'm telling you is my revenues don't go up faster than their revenues. I'm consuming more tokens every single day. Do I get more economic output? I am not.

summary: Jason frames the oil price volatility as significant and consequential, mapping out the spike from $84 to $119 and back, noting the Strait of Hormuz closure as an ongoing risk driver. His tone is descriptive/analytical rather than explicitly bullish or bearish, but he underscores the severity of the shock.
quote: Brent crude oil... it spiked to $84 on Friday... $119 on Monday... dropped back down to $84, jumped back up to $100 after 3 commercial ships were hit in the strait... Brent crude currently at $99 when we're taping this.

summary: Brad (Guest) argues the Trump doctrine is pragmatic and limited in scope, suggesting the conflict will be shorter in duration than feared, implying oil price spikes will be transient rather than sustained.
quote: I think the Trump doctrine is far more pragmatic than the neocon doctrine... my suspicion is that these impacts are shorter duration, but right now the market's having a little bit of post-traumatic stress flashbacks to Afghanistan and Iraq.

summary: Chamath interprets the market's sharp drop in oil from $120 to $90 on Trump's 'war over soon' comment as validation that sharps see no path to sustained conflict. He also highlights coordinated IEA strategic reserve releases (400M+ barrels) as a price dampener, concluding the worst is likely behind us.
quote: The market literally took oil from $120 a barrel to $90 a barrel... the fact that there was this reflexive move, I think is a belief by a lot of the Sharps that there is no path to a sustained conflict... I think the estimate is there's probably another billion or so more barrels that one could release out of strategic stockpiles.

summary: Sacks warns of significant oil price upside risk from escalation scenarios — Iranian tit-for-tat strikes on Gulf oil infrastructure could be far worse than the Strait closure alone — but favors de-escalation/declaring victory as the right path, which would be bullish for oil stabilization.
quote: If the Iranians get hit, if their oil and gas infrastructure gets hit, they've already said they're going to engage in tit-for-tat retaliation against the Gulf states... it won't really matter if the straits get reopened because you won't be able to restart oil and gas production in the Middle East.
